title: From user interviews to a clickable prototype

say: From user interviews to a clickable prototype.
This is the video for module 2 of UX Design Fundamentals.
In this module you move through the whole UX workflow on your own project.
You start by talking to 5 to 8 people who match your users. When you hear the same stories again and again, you have enough.

say: People are poor at predicting what they will do, but good at describing what they did.
Leading questions like these suggest the answer, so you only get a polite yes.

panel.heading: Ask about the past, not the future
left: Don't you find the app confusing?
Would you like a reminder feature?
right: Walk me through the last time
How do you remember appointments now?
How did you decide whether to pay?

say: Open questions start with what, how, or tell me about. Tell me about the last time you booked a fitting gets the truth.
Then listen more than you talk. People often add the most honest detail when they fill a pause.

say: For example, Blessing is redesigning bookings for a hair salon in Ikeja that takes bookings only on WhatsApp. She interviews 6 customers and writes 47 notes, one idea per note.

panel.heading: From notes to themes to a persona
items: Write one observation or quote per note
Group notes that are about the same thing
Name each group with a short theme
Count how many people mention each theme
Write a one-page persona from the themes

say: She groups the notes and names 5 themes, such as waiting for a reply, and price surprise. This is called affinity mapping.

panel.heading: From notes to themes to a persona
items: Write one observation or quote per note
Group notes that are about the same thing
Name each group with a short theme
Count how many people mention each theme
Write a one-page persona from the themes

say: Then she counts. 5 of 6 waited hours for the salon to confirm a slot. 4 of 6 learned the full price for braids only at the salon.
A theme 5 out of 6 people mention matters more than one mentioned once.

panel.heading: From notes to themes to a persona
items: Write one observation or quote per note

Name each group with a short theme
Count how many people mention each theme
Write a one-page persona from the themes

say: Finally, a one-page persona: goals, frustrations, device, habits and real quotes. A persona written before research is only a guess, so label it and replace it.

panel.heading: From notes to themes to a persona

Write a one-page persona from the themes
panel.rule: Build personas from research, never from imagination.

say: A journey map shows the task over time. In the salon map, she waits 3 hours for a price, is unsure the booking is confirmed, and finds her stylist double-booked.
Those low points are where design helps most.

cards.d: A timeline of what she does, thinks and feels. Design first for the lowest points.
Users group and name content cards, so your menu uses their words.
Screens, decisions and arrows for one task, including what happens when it goes wrong.

say: Card sorting shows how users group things. If they say hairstyles and the business says services, the menu should say hairstyles.

say: A user flow shows every screen and decision for one task. Draw the happy path first, then the error paths: slot taken, payment failed, network dropped.

say: Here is the flow Blessing draws. Screen 1 shows styles and prices. Screen 2 shows only free slots. If a slot is just taken, she sees a sorry message and keeps her chosen style.

panel.heading: Blessing's booking flow
items: Choose style, with photos and starting prices
Choose date and time: only free slots
Details: name and phone, two fields only
Pay deposit, with a clear amount
Confirmation with a reference number

say: Screen 3 asks only for name and phone. Every extra field is a chance to give up. If the deposit payment fails, she sees the reason and a try again button without losing her booking.

say: Screen 5 confirms the date, time, stylist, amount paid and a reference. Every pain point from the journey map now has an answer.

say: Next, Blessing builds two grey, mid-fidelity versions in Figma and asks 5 customers to book Saturday at 10am. With the month calendar, 3 of 5 scrolled past the slots and needed help.

panel.heading: Two wireframes for the time picker

say: With the row of days, all 5 booked without help, in about 20 seconds. She keeps Version B, and moves Confirm lower for easier thumb reach.
She compared two ideas in one afternoon, before spending any money on development.

panel.heading: Two wireframes for the time picker

say: Check every screen. Real labels like book appointment. One main action. The button where the thumb reaches. Big tap targets, about 44 to 48 units by platform guidelines.
The common mistake is jumping to colours before the flow works, and forgetting what the screen shows when there are no free slots.

panel.heading: Check every wireframe
items: Real labels, never placeholder text
One main action, darkest and largest
Main button in the lower half
Tap targets about 44 to 48 units
Empty and error states drawn
Checked on a small Android screen

say: To remember. Ask about real past behaviour. Count your themes. Design for the lowest points. Keep wireframes grey until the flow works, then link them in the Prototype tab and share the link for testing.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Open questions about real past behaviour
Count themes; build the persona from them
Fix the lowest points on the journey map
Grey wireframes first, colour last
Link screens in Figma's Prototype tab and share

say: Your turn. Interview, find your themes, and write your persona. Map the journey and the flow, sketch, and build your clickable prototype.
